notes: Only present simple, past simple and imperatives are used; no conditionals, relative clauses, passive or perfect forms.

A1 comprehension: apart from the glossed words, only 'frighten' ('He wanted to frighten the whole city.') and the phrase 'all over London' ('I can take it all over London.') are a bit above beginner level. Optional simpler versions: 'He wanted to make the whole city afraid.' and 'I can take it to every part of London.'
'The young man was in a cab already.' would sound a little more natural as 'The young man was already in a cab.'
Quiz keys are correct and each has only one defensible answer.
'He still had his house shoes on his feet.' 'House shoes' is understandable. 'He still had his slippers on.' is the more usual British wording if 'slippers' is glossed or accepted.
'Then he walked away among the people.' would read more naturally as 'Then he walked away into the crowd.'
Events, their order and the ending (the harmless blue microbe, Minnie and the coat) are faithful to Wells. Quiz keys are correct.
There are no conditionals or passives. 'One drop in the city water, and the sickness spreads...' is a noun phrase joined with 'and', not a formal conditional.

A few words are at the top of B1 range ('pedestrians', 'peculiar', 'trickled', 'chuckled', 'astonishment'). Optional simpler versions: 'People on the pavement stopped and laughed at the strange sight.'
Quiz keys match the text (slippers, frighten the whole city, people stopped and laughed).

'weeks of careful work had gone into it' and the later line 'I only found it last week' can be reconciled (weeks of work led to finding it), but a reader may pause. Optionally write 'and he had spent many careful days on it'.
''I did, and he believed every word,' said the Bacteriologist. The Bacteriologist began to laugh again.' The name is repeated in back-to-back sentences. Use 'He began to laugh again.'
'his precious new sample' hints at the twist before the reveal. This is acceptable, and it keeps the ending logical.

The same mild tension appears here: 'It had cost him weeks of patient work' and later 'that novelty I found last week'. It can be reconciled, but 'days of patient work' or 'I isolated last week' would remove any doubt.
'...said the Bacteriologist, "and he believed every syllable." The Bacteriologist began to laugh again.' The name is repeated. Use 'He began to laugh again.' for a smoother literary register.

'Pour it into the water supply of London, and within a few days the sickness would be running...' pairs an imperative with 'would'. Native speakers say this in speech, but 'will be running' is tidier.

'The young man in the first cab had no idea what he was really carrying.' gives the irony away early. Wells keeps the reveal for the end, so consider cutting the line, although it does not break the story.

The prose is genuinely literary and not padded. Minnie thinking he has gone mad, the slippers, the jeering cabmen, Waterloo Bridge, 'too late', and the kitten, three puppies and sparrow all match the original.

summary: All five levels faithfully retell Wells's 'The Stolen Bacillus': the cholera boast, the theft while Minnie calls her husband away, the three-cab chase, the broken tube drunk near Waterloo Bridge, and the reveal that the microbe only turns things blue. Grammar matches each level's limits and every quiz key is correct. The content suits a 4+ audience because the anarchist is softened and deaths are only mentioned as a threat. The remaining points are optional polish: the 'weeks of work' versus 'found last week' wording in B2 and C1, and the repeated 'The Bacteriologist' in the closing dialogue.
